plot_point: At dusk the shop is seventy percent full. The old regular Lu Wenfeng arrives, asking by the old rules for a quiet room, hot soup noodles, and half a jin of wine; only one Tianzi room remains, and Liu Sanniang has already quoted the price and arranged a solitary table by the window.

Lu Wenfeng explains that he came around from the Qixia Ferry side, and says that there have been more unfamiliar faces on the road, asking everyone they see about the old grain-transport gang. He asks in return whether Liu Sanniang has heard any rumors lately—routine pleasantries have turned into a probe for exchanging information.

Liu Sanniang reports the account as usual (a total of two qian and forty wen), blocks him back with “That depends on what kind of rumor it is,” then asks in return whether the unfamiliar face was asking toward the north or the south, handing the probe back to Lu Wenfeng. She immediately calls for noodles, cutting off the topic — the probing shifts from one-way to mutual weighing.

Lu Wenfeng answers that both north and south were questioned, and the most detailed questions were "who is alive, and where the ledgers ended up." He also points out that two of them were in plain clothes, but their boots were in the style of government runners, and at the end asks in return, "Have you taken in guests like this in the past half year?"—the signal that the authorities are intervening in the old case is laid out in the open, and the probing points directly at Banhuchun Inn itself.

Liu Sanniang openly lays down a rule with “Guests who have stayed here—I don’t talk about them,” then leaves a crack with “it’s not about a guest,” turning the thread away from the guest’s whereabouts; immediately afterward, she uses the old topic of the latch on the Tianzi room to bring up sworn brothers, pauses halfway through, then reins it in with “I’ve always been too lazy to fix it” and turns to walk inside—boundary-setting and something close to a slip of the tongue coexist, as the probing shifts into the substantive threat of “whether the inn itself has been tampered with.”

Lu Wenfeng picks up “the rules weren’t broken” and moves the topic from the main hall upstairs: after finishing the noodles, they will go upstairs, and he asks Liu Sanniang to bring a pot of tea when she is free, saying plainly, “I have an old object that may be related to that sworn brother of yours”—the old-case clue is handed over directly, and the conversation is arranged for a private space behind closed doors, upgrading the probing into the handover of a physical object from the old case.

Liu Sanniang’s steps pause; she turns back and stands still, asking in a low voice, “You’re not saying this to trade for the room money, are you?”—leaving Lu Wenfeng a step down to retract it. Seeing that his expression does not change, she nods and agrees, “Noodles in a quarter of an hour. After you finish eating, go upstairs; I’ll personally bring the tea over”, then turns into the inner room and waves to Old Zhao to signal that nothing is wrong—the private-room handoff has been agreed upon, only awaiting going upstairs.

Lu Wenfeng's line “No” closes off the escape route, then he adds “old objects don't pay for the room; only old people count” and “shut the door”—the sincerity and privacy of the private conversation are nailed down, and the handover only awaits the noodles being finished and the person going upstairs.

Liu Sanniang places a handkerchief on the corner of the table to separate them from others, goes into the inner room and waves to Old Zhao to indicate nothing is wrong, then, once alone, stands at the back courtyard threshold looking at the boat lights, and returns to the kitchen to ladle water and set up the stove herself, waiting for the water to boil—a silent preparation before the private talk, only waiting for the noodles to be finished and the person to go upstairs.

Lu Wenfeng finishes the noodles and goes upstairs; Liu Sanniang brings tea into the room. Lu Wenfeng bars the door, takes a charred Canal Gang waist token from inside his robe, places it on the table, and states plainly, “the owner of this object is still alive” and “the account book from that year did not sink at Qixia Ferry”—the physical evidence from the old case and the clue to a living witness are handed over face to face, and the private talk moves from agreement into substance.

Liu Sanniang picked up the waist token and turned it over to look at the back. She recognized the knife-carved private notch in the lower right corner; her finger stopped on the notch for a long while before she put it back on the table. She only asked the four words "Where is he," then pushed the door bolt firmly shut and sat down across from Lu Wenfeng, waiting for him to speak—the old case advanced from "showing the physical object" to "confirming the private mark and asking about the survivor’s whereabouts," and the private conversation entered substantive questioning and answering.

Lu Wenfeng gives the location of the surviving witness: the abandoned Dragon King Temple seven li south of the city; the survivor is badly injured and will only see Liu Sanniang; go by the back door before the third watch, and bring no one else; as for whose hands the account book is in, he will say it face to face—the old case advances from "asking after the survivor's whereabouts" to "agreeing to personally go to the abandoned temple at the third watch tonight to meet the survivor," and the private conversation enters an action agreement.

Liu Sanniang presses Lu Wenfeng on whether he was entrusted by someone or stumbled upon it himself; without waiting for him to answer, she states, “It is not that I do not trust you; it is that before I go, I must think the matter through clearly”. She then rises, leaves the window cracked, tucks the waist token into the cloth pouch at her chest, and says in a low voice, “I do not care whose hands the ledger falls into. I only want to know who set that fire back then”. At the end, she lifts the door latch, her expression already calm, and says, “Before the third watch, I will go myself”—the action agreement advances from “waiting for her nod” to “she has accepted this trip, and is pressing for the source of the clue”.

Lu Wenfeng answers that this lead was entrusted to him by a surviving witness: he ran into the witness at the ferry crossing while they were being hunted, and shielded them for a stretch. He also explains that someone is watching the southern road, that they should take the old mulberry grove along the river embankment, that he himself will not enter the temple but will wait half a li away, and that if the witness has not come out after the time it takes one incense stick to burn, he will not keep to the witness's rules—the source of the clue and tonight's pickup arrangements are both laid out together, advancing the private talk from "questioning the source" to "jointly discussing how to go tonight."

Liu Sanniang stops at the doorway, links together “shielded him for a stretch” with the dark stain on the right sleeve and the dust from the road, and acknowledges this favor; then she turns and says, “The old mulberry grove on the riverbank—I have walked it, I remember”, and advises Lu Wenfeng, “You need not wait tonight”—marking the matter at the temple as “my own affair”, fearing that if he runs into people from the southern road, he will instead become trouble; at the end, she slides the door bolt back into place and sets the limit, “One incense stick. If I cannot come out, then make your own decision”—the support arrangement is contracted from “wait half a li away” to “you need not wait, one incense stick as the limit”, and the private talk enters the closing phase of action preparation.

Lu Wenfeng answers, “Fine,” releases the sword sheath, and says lightly, “I’ll sleep mine, you walk yours. As for whether someone is enjoying the cool air half a li away, that is not under the innkeeper’s jurisdiction”—the reception arrangement settles from “you need not wait; the limit is one incense stick” into “he sleeps his, she walks hers, and he will watch the matter half a li away himself.” The private talk draws to a close, only awaiting the third watch.

Liu Sanniang did not push again, nor did she thank him; she only lifted the teapot again and refilled half a cup, gave the ordinary reminder, 'Don't drink too much before bed,' walked to the door and paused, said softly, 'Thank you,' then closed the door behind her and went downstairs—the private conversation formally concludes, shifting into the wait before the third watch.

Liu Sanniang goes downstairs and sits down behind the counter, picks up the ledger, and flips through two pages without taking anything in. The river wind seeping in through the crack in the window is cool—there are still two hours until the third watch, and action preparation shifts into quiet waiting.

It was nearly the third watch. Lu Wenfeng made no reply, only blew out the lamp, quietly went out the back door, and arrived at the old mulberry grove one step ahead—his mouth said “not under the innkeeper’s control,” yet his feet went there before her, quietly taking up the boundary she had drawn; on Liu Sanniang’s side, all that remained was to hurry on the road. The time had come to go out the back door before the third watch and go in person to the abandoned temple.

If you two are out enjoying the cool air, choose another patch of woods"—the watchers on the southern road had already reached the edge of the mulberry grove, and the contact had blocked the way outside the temple one step ahead; the road to the temple was cut off.

plot_point: At dusk the shop is seventy percent full. The old regular Lu Wenfeng arrives, asking by the old rules for a quiet room, hot soup noodles, and half a jin of wine; only one Tianzi room remains, and Liu Sanniang has already quoted the price and arranged a solitary table by the window.

Lu Wenfeng explains that he came around from the Qixia Ferry side, and says that there have been more unfamiliar faces on the road, asking everyone they see about the old grain-transport gang. He asks in return whether Liu Sanniang has heard any rumors lately—routine pleasantries have turned into a probe for exchanging information.

Liu Sanniang reports the account as usual (a total of two qian and forty wen), blocks him back with “That depends on what kind of rumor it is,” then asks in return whether the unfamiliar face was asking toward the north or the south, handing the probe back to Lu Wenfeng. She immediately calls for noodles, cutting off the topic — the probing shifts from one-way to mutual weighing.

Lu Wenfeng answers that both north and south were questioned, and the most detailed questions were "who is alive, and where the ledgers ended up." He also points out that two of them were in plain clothes, but their boots were in the style of government runners, and at the end asks in return, "Have you taken in guests like this in the past half year?"—the signal that the authorities are intervening in the old case is laid out in the open, and the probing points directly at Banhuchun Inn itself.

Liu Sanniang openly lays down a rule with “Guests who have stayed here—I don’t talk about them,” then leaves a crack with “it’s not about a guest,” turning the thread away from the guest’s whereabouts; immediately afterward, she uses the old topic of the latch on the Tianzi room to bring up sworn brothers, pauses halfway through, then reins it in with “I’ve always been too lazy to fix it” and turns to walk inside—boundary-setting and something close to a slip of the tongue coexist, as the probing shifts into the substantive threat of “whether the inn itself has been tampered with.”

Lu Wenfeng picks up “the rules weren’t broken” and moves the topic from the main hall upstairs: after finishing the noodles, they will go upstairs, and he asks Liu Sanniang to bring a pot of tea when she is free, saying plainly, “I have an old object that may be related to that sworn brother of yours”—the old-case clue is handed over directly, and the conversation is arranged for a private space behind closed doors, upgrading the probing into the handover of a physical object from the old case.

Liu Sanniang’s steps pause; she turns back and stands still, asking in a low voice, “You’re not saying this to trade for the room money, are you?”—leaving Lu Wenfeng a step down to retract it. Seeing that his expression does not change, she nods and agrees, “Noodles in a quarter of an hour. After you finish eating, go upstairs; I’ll personally bring the tea over”, then turns into the inner room and waves to Old Zhao to signal that nothing is wrong—the private-room handoff has been agreed upon, only awaiting going upstairs.

Lu Wenfeng's line “No” closes off the escape route, then he adds “old objects don't pay for the room; only old people count” and “shut the door”—the sincerity and privacy of the private conversation are nailed down, and the handover only awaits the noodles being finished and the person going upstairs.

Liu Sanniang places a handkerchief on the corner of the table to separate them from others, goes into the inner room and waves to Old Zhao to indicate nothing is wrong, then, once alone, stands at the back courtyard threshold looking at the boat lights, and returns to the kitchen to ladle water and set up the stove herself, waiting for the water to boil—a silent preparation before the private talk, only waiting for the noodles to be finished and the person to go upstairs.

Lu Wenfeng finishes the noodles and goes upstairs; Liu Sanniang brings tea into the room. Lu Wenfeng bars the door, takes a charred Canal Gang waist token from inside his robe, places it on the table, and states plainly, “the owner of this object is still alive” and “the account book from that year did not sink at Qixia Ferry”—the physical evidence from the old case and the clue to a living witness are handed over face to face, and the private talk moves from agreement into substance.

Liu Sanniang picked up the waist token and turned it over to look at the back. She recognized the knife-carved private notch in the lower right corner; her finger stopped on the notch for a long while before she put it back on the table. She only asked the four words "Where is he," then pushed the door bolt firmly shut and sat down across from Lu Wenfeng, waiting for him to speak—the old case advanced from "showing the physical object" to "confirming the private mark and asking about the survivor’s whereabouts," and the private conversation entered substantive questioning and answering.

Lu Wenfeng gives the location of the surviving witness: the abandoned Dragon King Temple seven li south of the city; the survivor is badly injured and will only see Liu Sanniang; go by the back door before the third watch, and bring no one else; as for whose hands the account book is in, he will say it face to face—the old case advances from "asking after the survivor's whereabouts" to "agreeing to personally go to the abandoned temple at the third watch tonight to meet the survivor," and the private conversation enters an action agreement.

Liu Sanniang presses Lu Wenfeng on whether he was entrusted by someone or stumbled upon it himself; without waiting for him to answer, she states, “It is not that I do not trust you; it is that before I go, I must think the matter through clearly”. She then rises, leaves the window cracked, tucks the waist token into the cloth pouch at her chest, and says in a low voice, “I do not care whose hands the ledger falls into. I only want to know who set that fire back then”. At the end, she lifts the door latch, her expression already calm, and says, “Before the third watch, I will go myself”—the action agreement advances from “waiting for her nod” to “she has accepted this trip, and is pressing for the source of the clue”.

Lu Wenfeng answers that this lead was entrusted to him by a surviving witness: he ran into the witness at the ferry crossing while they were being hunted, and shielded them for a stretch. He also explains that someone is watching the southern road, that they should take the old mulberry grove along the river embankment, that he himself will not enter the temple but will wait half a li away, and that if the witness has not come out after the time it takes one incense stick to burn, he will not keep to the witness's rules—the source of the clue and tonight's pickup arrangements are both laid out together, advancing the private talk from "questioning the source" to "jointly discussing how to go tonight."

Liu Sanniang stops at the doorway, links together “shielded him for a stretch” with the dark stain on the right sleeve and the dust from the road, and acknowledges this favor; then she turns and says, “The old mulberry grove on the riverbank—I have walked it, I remember”, and advises Lu Wenfeng, “You need not wait tonight”—marking the matter at the temple as “my own affair”, fearing that if he runs into people from the southern road, he will instead become trouble; at the end, she slides the door bolt back into place and sets the limit, “One incense stick. If I cannot come out, then make your own decision”—the support arrangement is contracted from “wait half a li away” to “you need not wait, one incense stick as the limit”, and the private talk enters the closing phase of action preparation.

Lu Wenfeng answers, “Fine,” releases the sword sheath, and says lightly, “I’ll sleep mine, you walk yours. As for whether someone is enjoying the cool air half a li away, that is not under the innkeeper’s jurisdiction”—the reception arrangement settles from “you need not wait; the limit is one incense stick” into “he sleeps his, she walks hers, and he will watch the matter half a li away himself.” The private talk draws to a close, only awaiting the third watch.

Liu Sanniang did not push again, nor did she thank him; she only lifted the teapot again and refilled half a cup, gave the ordinary reminder, 'Don't drink too much before bed,' walked to the door and paused, said softly, 'Thank you,' then closed the door behind her and went downstairs—the private conversation formally concludes, shifting into the wait before the third watch.

Liu Sanniang goes downstairs and sits down behind the counter, picks up the ledger, and flips through two pages without taking anything in. The river wind seeping in through the crack in the window is cool—there are still two hours until the third watch, and action preparation shifts into quiet waiting.

It was nearly the third watch. Lu Wenfeng made no reply, only blew out the lamp, quietly went out the back door, and arrived at the old mulberry grove one step ahead—his mouth said “not under the innkeeper’s control,” yet his feet went there before her, quietly taking up the boundary she had drawn; on Liu Sanniang’s side, all that remained was to hurry on the road. The time had come to go out the back door before the third watch and go in person to the abandoned temple.

Liu Sanniang gropes her way to the edge of the old mulberry grove in the dark, stops and listens for a moment, discerns that there is a cloth-covered dim lamp in the temple's direction and that the south side and the riverbank are both quiet, glimpses the outline of Lu Wenfeng's sword sheath in the woods, pauses toward him briefly as a greeting, then unties the sash of her outer robe, grips the waist token in her palm to warm it, and strides toward the ruined temple—the person has already set out from the edge of the mulberry grove, and the temple gate is in sight.

Liu Sanniang had only counted to twenty breaths when two dark figures came feeling their way along the southern slope, the sound of their boot soles treading mud the same as that group at the ferry crossing; Lu Wenfeng held his sword across their path and said in a low voice, "It is late. If you two are out enjoying the cool air, choose another patch of woods"—the watchers on the southern road had already reached the edge of the mulberry grove, and the contact had blocked the way outside the temple one step ahead; the road to the temple was cut off.

Liu Sanniang steps over the threshold of the ruined temple. From the direction of the mulberry grove behind her come muffled footsteps and an extremely low sentence, broken and intermittent, but that direction is Lu Wenfeng. She clenches the waist tag and does not look back, striding into the temple—the two lines inside and outside the temple advance simultaneously.

Inside the ruined temple, the incense table has long since collapsed, mud swallow nests hang from the beams, and someone is leaning in the corner, covering a bean-sized lamp with cloth; the breathing is very shallow, but present. Liu Sanniang walks over and crouches down, says in a low voice, “It’s me,” and spreads the charred waist token in the lamplight for him to see for himself, her eyes looking only at the person before her as she waits for him to speak—the temple interior advances from “entering the temple” to “facing a living survivor, laying the cards on the table and identifying each other.”

Lu Wenfeng’s sword is still not unsheathed; it only lies across his knees as he upgrades the soft phrasing of ‘change to another patch of woods’ into the overt threat, ‘Take one more step forward, and “enjoying the shade” will have to become “lying in the cool,”’ and presses further: ‘Who sent you here?’—the confrontation outside the temple advances from ‘blocking the road to pass along a message’ to ‘questioning them to their faces and forcing the other side to account for where they came from,’ while the two lines of questioning the case inside the temple and coercing a confession outside the temple both enter substantive confrontation.

Liu Sanniang crouched in front of the live captive, clutching the waist token in her hand, her ears pricked toward the outside. Hearing that Lu Wenfeng had not drawn his sword and was forcing answers out of them, she split half her attention outside and asked the captive in a low voice, “How long have they been following?”—the temple inquiry advances from “showdown and identification” to “asking where the people outside came from,” and the two lines of inquiry inside the temple and coercive questioning outside the temple simultaneously enter substantive confrontation.

As for whether anyone is enjoying the cool air half a li away, that is not under the innkeeper’s jurisdiction”—gently setting the topic of backup back down, both acknowledging her boundary-drawing and keeping his own fallback.

Liu Sanniang did not push any further, nor did she thank him; she only picked up the teapot again and refilled half a cup, gave an ordinary reminder, "Don't drink too much before bed," paused at the doorway, said softly, "Thank you," and then closed the door behind her and went downstairs.

Liu Sanniang went downstairs and sat down behind the counter, picked up the account book, and flipped through two pages without taking anything in. The river wind seeping through the crack in the window was cool—there were still two double-hours before the third watch.

Lu Wenfeng did not answer; he only blew out the lamp. Near the third watch, he quietly went out the back door and arrived at the old mulberry grove one step ahead—his mouth said “not under the innkeeper's management”, but his feet went there before she did, quietly taking up the boundary she had drawn.

Liu Sanniang gropes her way to the edge of the old mulberry grove in the dark, stops and listens for a moment, discerns that there is a cloth-covered dim lamp in the temple's direction and that the south side and the riverbank are both quiet, glimpses the outline of Lu Wenfeng's sword sheath in the woods, pauses toward him briefly as a greeting, then unties the sash of her outer robe, grips the waist token in her palm to warm it, and strides toward the ruined temple—the person has already set out from the edge of the mulberry grove, and the temple gate is in sight.

Liu Sanniang had only counted to twenty breaths when two dark figures felt their way over from the south slope, the sound of their boot soles stepping in mud just like that group at the ferry. Lu Wenfeng held his sword across the path and blocked the way, saying in a low voice, “It is late. If you two are out enjoying the cool air, choose another patch of woods”—the watchers on the southern route had already reached the edge of the mulberry grove, and the contact had blocked the way outside the temple one step ahead.

Liu Sanniang stepped over the threshold of the ruined temple. From the direction of the mulberry grove behind her came muffled footsteps and a very low sentence, broken and intermittent, but that direction was Lu Wenfeng; she clenched the waist token and did not look back, striding into the temple.

Inside the abandoned temple, the incense table had long since collapsed, and mud swallow nests hung from the beams. Someone was leaning in the corner, with a lamp the size of a bean covered by cloth; the breathing was very shallow, but present. Liu Sanniang walked over and crouched down, said softly, “It’s me,” and spread the charred waist tablet in the lamplight for him to see for himself, her eyes looking only at the person before her, waiting for him to speak.

Lu Wenfeng's sword is still not drawn; he merely lays it horizontally before his knees, upgrading the soft talk of “finding another patch of woods” into the explicit threat of “take one more step forward, and cooling off in the shade will have to become lying there cold,” then presses, “Who sent you here?”—the confrontation outside the temple advances from “blocking the road to pass on a message” to “questioning them face to face and forcing them to explain where they came from.”

Liu Sanniang crouched in front of the live captive, clutching the waist token in her hand, her ears pricked toward the outside. Hearing that Lu Wenfeng had not drawn his sword and was forcing answers out of them, she split half her attention outside and asked the captive in a low voice, “How long have they been following?”—the temple inquiry advances from “showdown and identification” to “asking where the people outside came from,” and the two lines of inquiry inside the temple and coercive questioning outside the temple simultaneously enter substantive confrontation.

plot_point: At dusk the shop is seventy percent full. The old regular Lu Wenfeng arrives, asking by the old rules for a quiet room, hot soup noodles, and half a jin of wine; only one Tianzi room remains, and Liu Sanniang has already quoted the price and arranged a solitary table by the window.

Lu Wenfeng explains that he came around from the Qixia Ferry side, and says that there have been more unfamiliar faces on the road, asking everyone they see about the old grain-transport gang. He asks in return whether Liu Sanniang has heard any rumors lately—routine pleasantries have turned into a probe for exchanging information.

Liu Sanniang reports the account as usual (a total of two qian and forty wen), blocks him back with “That depends on what kind of rumor it is,” then asks in return whether the unfamiliar face was asking toward the north or the south, handing the probe back to Lu Wenfeng. She immediately calls for noodles, cutting off the topic — the probing shifts from one-way to mutual weighing.

Lu Wenfeng answers that both north and south were questioned, and the most detailed questions were "who is alive, and where the ledgers ended up." He also points out that two of them were in plain clothes, but their boots were in the style of government runners, and at the end asks in return, "Have you taken in guests like this in the past half year?"—the signal that the authorities are intervening in the old case is laid out in the open, and the probing points directly at Banhuchun Inn itself.

Liu Sanniang openly lays down a rule with “Guests who have stayed here—I don’t talk about them,” then leaves a crack with “it’s not about a guest,” turning the thread away from the guest’s whereabouts; immediately afterward, she uses the old topic of the latch on the Tianzi room to bring up sworn brothers, pauses halfway through, then reins it in with “I’ve always been too lazy to fix it” and turns to walk inside—boundary-setting and something close to a slip of the tongue coexist, as the probing shifts into the substantive threat of “whether the inn itself has been tampered with.”

Lu Wenfeng picks up “the rules weren’t broken” and moves the topic from the main hall upstairs: after finishing the noodles, they will go upstairs, and he asks Liu Sanniang to bring a pot of tea when she is free, saying plainly, “I have an old object that may be related to that sworn brother of yours”—the old-case clue is handed over directly, and the conversation is arranged for a private space behind closed doors, upgrading the probing into the handover of a physical object from the old case.

Liu Sanniang’s steps pause; she turns back and stands still, asking in a low voice, “You’re not saying this to trade for the room money, are you?”—leaving Lu Wenfeng a step down to retract it. Seeing that his expression does not change, she nods and agrees, “Noodles in a quarter of an hour. After you finish eating, go upstairs; I’ll personally bring the tea over”, then turns into the inner room and waves to Old Zhao to signal that nothing is wrong—the private-room handoff has been agreed upon, only awaiting going upstairs.

Lu Wenfeng's line “No” closes off the escape route, then he adds “old objects don't pay for the room; only old people count” and “shut the door”—the sincerity and privacy of the private conversation are nailed down, and the handover only awaits the noodles being finished and the person going upstairs.

Liu Sanniang places a handkerchief on the corner of the table to separate them from others, goes into the inner room and waves to Old Zhao to indicate nothing is wrong, then, once alone, stands at the back courtyard threshold looking at the boat lights, and returns to the kitchen to ladle water and set up the stove herself, waiting for the water to boil—a silent preparation before the private talk, only waiting for the noodles to be finished and the person to go upstairs.

Lu Wenfeng finishes the noodles and goes upstairs; Liu Sanniang brings tea into the room. Lu Wenfeng bars the door, takes a charred Canal Gang waist token from inside his robe, places it on the table, and states plainly, “the owner of this object is still alive” and “the account book from that year did not sink at Qixia Ferry”—the physical evidence from the old case and the clue to a living witness are handed over face to face, and the private talk moves from agreement into substance.

Liu Sanniang picked up the waist token and turned it over to look at the back. She recognized the knife-carved private notch in the lower right corner; her finger stopped on the notch for a long while before she put it back on the table. She only asked the four words "Where is he," then pushed the door bolt firmly shut and sat down across from Lu Wenfeng, waiting for him to speak—the old case advanced from "showing the physical object" to "confirming the private mark and asking about the survivor’s whereabouts," and the private conversation entered substantive questioning and answering.

Lu Wenfeng gives the location of the surviving witness: the abandoned Dragon King Temple seven li south of the city; the survivor is badly injured and will only see Liu Sanniang; go by the back door before the third watch, and bring no one else; as for whose hands the account book is in, he will say it face to face—the old case advances from "asking after the survivor's whereabouts" to "agreeing to personally go to the abandoned temple at the third watch tonight to meet the survivor," and the private conversation enters an action agreement.

Liu Sanniang presses Lu Wenfeng on whether he was entrusted by someone or stumbled upon it himself; without waiting for him to answer, she states, “It is not that I do not trust you; it is that before I go, I must think the matter through clearly”. She then rises, leaves the window cracked, tucks the waist token into the cloth pouch at her chest, and says in a low voice, “I do not care whose hands the ledger falls into. I only want to know who set that fire back then”. At the end, she lifts the door latch, her expression already calm, and says, “Before the third watch, I will go myself”—the action agreement advances from “waiting for her nod” to “she has accepted this trip, and is pressing for the source of the clue”.

Lu Wenfeng answers that this lead was entrusted to him by a surviving witness: he ran into the witness at the ferry crossing while they were being hunted, and shielded them for a stretch. He also explains that someone is watching the southern road, that they should take the old mulberry grove along the river embankment, that he himself will not enter the temple but will wait half a li away, and that if the witness has not come out after the time it takes one incense stick to burn, he will not keep to the witness's rules—the source of the clue and tonight's pickup arrangements are both laid out together, advancing the private talk from "questioning the source" to "jointly discussing how to go tonight."

Liu Sanniang stops at the doorway, links together “shielded him for a stretch” with the dark stain on the right sleeve and the dust from the road, and acknowledges this favor; then she turns and says, “The old mulberry grove on the riverbank—I have walked it, I remember”, and advises Lu Wenfeng, “You need not wait tonight”—marking the matter at the temple as “my own affair”, fearing that if he runs into people from the southern road, he will instead become trouble; at the end, she slides the door bolt back into place and sets the limit, “One incense stick. plot_point: At dusk the shop is seventy percent full. The old regular Lu Wenfeng arrives, asking by the old rules for a quiet room, hot soup noodles, and half a jin of wine; only one Tianzi room remains, and Liu Sanniang has already quoted the price and arranged a solitary table by the window.

Lu Wenfeng explains that he came around from the Qixia Ferry side, and says that there have been more unfamiliar faces on the road, asking everyone they see about the old grain-transport gang. He asks in return whether Liu Sanniang has heard any rumors lately—routine pleasantries have turned into a probe for exchanging information.

Liu Sanniang reports the account as usual (a total of two qian and forty wen), blocks him back with “That depends on what kind of rumor it is,” then asks in return whether the unfamiliar face was asking toward the north or the south, handing the probe back to Lu Wenfeng. She immediately calls for noodles, cutting off the topic — the probing shifts from one-way to mutual weighing.

Lu Wenfeng answers that both north and south were questioned, and the most detailed questions were "who is alive, and where the ledgers ended up." He also points out that two of them were in plain clothes, but their boots were in the style of government runners, and at the end asks in return, "Have you taken in guests like this in the past half year?"—the signal that the authorities are intervening in the old case is laid out in the open, and the probing points directly at Banhuchun Inn itself.

Liu Sanniang openly lays down a rule with “Guests who have stayed here—I don’t talk about them,” then leaves a crack with “it’s not about a guest,” turning the thread away from the guest’s whereabouts; immediately afterward, she uses the old topic of the latch on the Tianzi room to bring up sworn brothers, pauses halfway through, then reins it in with “I’ve always been too lazy to fix it” and turns to walk inside—boundary-setting and something close to a slip of the tongue coexist, as the probing shifts into the substantive threat of “whether the inn itself has been tampered with.”

Lu Wenfeng picks up “the rules weren’t broken” and moves the topic from the main hall upstairs: after finishing the noodles, they will go upstairs, and he asks Liu Sanniang to bring a pot of tea when she is free, saying plainly, “I have an old object that may be related to that sworn brother of yours”—the old-case clue is handed over directly, and the conversation is arranged for a private space behind closed doors, upgrading the probing into the handover of a physical object from the old case.

Liu Sanniang’s steps pause; she turns back and stands still, asking in a low voice, “You’re not saying this to trade for the room money, are you?”—leaving Lu Wenfeng a step down to retract it. Seeing that his expression does not change, she nods and agrees, “Noodles in a quarter of an hour. After you finish eating, go upstairs; I’ll personally bring the tea over”, then turns into the inner room and waves to Old Zhao to signal that nothing is wrong—the private-room handoff has been agreed upon, only awaiting going upstairs.

Lu Wenfeng's line “No” closes off the escape route, then he adds “old objects don't pay for the room; only old people count” and “shut the door”—the sincerity and privacy of the private conversation are nailed down, and the handover only awaits the noodles being finished and the person going upstairs.

Liu Sanniang places a handkerchief on the corner of the table to separate them from others, goes into the inner room and waves to Old Zhao to indicate nothing is wrong, then, once alone, stands at the back courtyard threshold looking at the boat lights, and returns to the kitchen to ladle water and set up the stove herself, waiting for the water to boil—a silent preparation before the private talk, only waiting for the noodles to be finished and the person to go upstairs.

Lu Wenfeng finishes the noodles and goes upstairs; Liu Sanniang brings tea into the room. Lu Wenfeng bars the door, takes a charred Canal Gang waist token from inside his robe, places it on the table, and states plainly, “the owner of this object is still alive” and “the account book from that year did not sink at Qixia Ferry”—the physical evidence from the old case and the clue to a living witness are handed over face to face, and the private talk moves from agreement into substance.

Liu Sanniang picked up the waist token and turned it over to look at the back. She recognized the knife-carved private notch in the lower right corner; her finger stopped on the notch for a long while before she put it back on the table. She only asked the four words "Where is he," then pushed the door bolt firmly shut and sat down across from Lu Wenfeng, waiting for him to speak—the old case advanced from "showing the physical object" to "confirming the private mark and asking about the survivor’s whereabouts," and the private conversation entered substantive questioning and answering.

Lu Wenfeng gives the location of the surviving witness: the abandoned Dragon King Temple seven li south of the city; the survivor is badly injured and will only see Liu Sanniang; go by the back door before the third watch, and bring no one else; as for whose hands the account book is in, he will say it face to face—the old case advances from "asking after the survivor's whereabouts" to "agreeing to personally go to the abandoned temple at the third watch tonight to meet the survivor," and the private conversation enters an action agreement.

Liu Sanniang presses Lu Wenfeng on whether he was entrusted by someone or stumbled upon it himself; without waiting for him to answer, she states, “It is not that I do not trust you; it is that before I go, I must think the matter through clearly”. She then rises, leaves the window cracked, tucks the waist token into the cloth pouch at her chest, and says in a low voice, “I do not care whose hands the ledger falls into. I only want to know who set that fire back then”. At the end, she lifts the door latch, her expression already calm, and says, “Before the third watch, I will go myself”—the action agreement advances from “waiting for her nod” to “she has accepted this trip, and is pressing for the source of the clue”.

Lu Wenfeng answers that this lead was entrusted to him by a surviving witness: he ran into the witness at the ferry crossing while they were being hunted, and shielded them for a stretch. He also explains that someone is watching the southern road, that they should take the old mulberry grove along the river embankment, that he himself will not enter the temple but will wait half a li away, and that if the witness has not come out after the time it takes one incense stick to burn, he will not keep to the witness's rules—the source of the clue and tonight's pickup arrangements are both laid out together, advancing the private talk from "questioning the source" to "jointly discussing how to go tonight."

Liu Sanniang stops at the doorway, links together “shielded him for a stretch” with the dark stain on the right sleeve and the dust from the road, and acknowledges this favor; then she turns and says, “The old mulberry grove on the riverbank—I have walked it, I remember”, and advises Lu Wenfeng, “You need not wait tonight”—marking the matter at the temple as “my own affair”, fearing that if he runs into people from the southern road, he will instead become trouble; at the end, she slides the door bolt back into place and sets the limit, “One incense stick. If I cannot come out, then make your own decision”—the support arrangement is contracted from “wait half a li away” to “you need not wait, one incense stick as the limit”, and the private talk enters the closing phase of action preparation.

Lu Wenfeng answers, “Fine,” releases the sword sheath, and says lightly, “I’ll sleep mine, you walk yours. As for whether someone is enjoying the cool air half a li away, that is not under the innkeeper’s jurisdiction”—the reception arrangement settles from “you need not wait; the limit is one incense stick” into “he sleeps his, she walks hers, and he will watch the matter half a li away himself.” The private talk draws to a close, only awaiting the third watch.

Liu Sanniang did not push again, nor did she thank him; she only lifted the teapot again and refilled half a cup, gave the ordinary reminder, 'Don't drink too much before bed,' walked to the door and paused, said softly, 'Thank you,' then closed the door behind her and went downstairs—the private conversation formally concludes, shifting into the wait before the third watch.

Liu Sanniang goes downstairs and sits down behind the counter, picks up the ledger, and flips through two pages without taking anything in. The river wind seeping in through the crack in the window is cool—there are still two hours until the third watch, and action preparation shifts into quiet waiting.

It was nearly the third watch. Lu Wenfeng made no reply, only blew out the lamp, quietly went out the back door, and arrived at the old mulberry grove one step ahead—his mouth said “not under the innkeeper’s control,” yet his feet went there before her, quietly taking up the boundary she had drawn; on Liu Sanniang’s side, all that remained was to hurry on the road. The time had come to go out the back door before the third watch and go in person to the abandoned temple.

Liu Sanniang gropes her way to the edge of the old mulberry grove in the dark, stops and listens for a moment, discerns that there is a cloth-covered dim lamp in the temple's direction and that the south side and the riverbank are both quiet, glimpses the outline of Lu Wenfeng's sword sheath in the woods, pauses toward him briefly as a greeting, then unties the sash of her outer robe, grips the waist token in her palm to warm it, and strides toward the ruined temple—the person has already set out from the edge of the mulberry grove, and the temple gate is in sight.

Liu Sanniang had only counted to twenty breaths when two dark figures came feeling their way along the southern slope, the sound of their boot soles treading mud the same as that group at the ferry crossing; Lu Wenfeng held his sword across their path and said in a low voice, "It is late. If you two are out enjoying the cool air, choose another patch of woods"—the watchers on the southern road had already reached the edge of the mulberry grove, and the contact had blocked the way outside the temple one step ahead; the road to the temple was cut off.

Liu Sanniang steps over the threshold of the ruined temple. From the direction of the mulberry grove behind her come muffled footsteps and an extremely low sentence, broken and intermittent, but that direction is Lu Wenfeng. She clenches the waist tag and does not look back, striding into the temple—the two lines inside and outside the temple advance simultaneously.

Inside the ruined temple, the incense table has long since collapsed, mud swallow nests hang from the beams, and someone is leaning in the corner, covering a bean-sized lamp with cloth; the breathing is very shallow, but present. Liu Sanniang walks over and crouches down, says in a low voice, “It’s me,” and spreads the charred waist token in the lamplight for him to see for himself, her eyes looking only at the person before her as she waits for him to speak—the temple interior advances from “entering the temple” to “facing a living survivor, laying the cards on the table and identifying each other.”

Lu Wenfeng’s sword is still not unsheathed; it only lies across his knees as he upgrades the soft phrasing of ‘change to another patch of woods’ into the overt threat, ‘Take one more step forward, and “enjoying the shade” will have to become “lying in the cool,”’ and presses further: ‘Who sent you here?’—the confrontation outside the temple advances from ‘blocking the road to pass along a message’ to ‘questioning them to their faces and forcing the other side to account for where they came from,’ while the two lines of questioning the case inside the temple and coercing a confession outside the temple both enter substantive confrontation.

Liu Sanniang crouched in front of the live captive, clutching the waist token in her hand, her ears pricked toward the outside. Hearing that Lu Wenfeng had not drawn his sword and was forcing answers out of them, she split half her attention outside and asked the captive in a low voice, “How long have they been following?”—the temple inquiry advances from “showdown and identification” to “asking where the people outside came from,” and the two lines of inquiry inside the temple and coercive questioning outside the temple simultaneously enter substantive confrontation.

Lu Wenfeng counts out three breaths, presses the sword edge against the throat to force a confession, and the survivor in the temple spits out “the Canal Transport Gang” and “the new boss” under the lamp—the mastermind points toward their own people. The interrogation outside the temple has half succeeded, and the inquiry inside the temple advances from “asking about the outside origin” to “a name pointing inside the gang”; Liu Sanniang’s twelve-year suspicion of an “inside traitor” is half confirmed to her face.

goal_tracking.underlying_goal: One possible deeper motive: to use the waist token and living-witness clue handed over by Lu Wenfeng to investigate clearly the old case of the fire at Qixia Ferry twelve years ago, in order to protect the rear-yard message relay point and the truth behind his sworn brother's death.
evidence: Liu Sanniang pressed Lu Wenfeng: “On this trip, were you entrusted by him, or did you stumble upon it yourself?”—without waiting for him to answer, she laid out her reason herself: “It’s not that I don’t trust you. It’s that before I go, I have to think the matter through clearly,” treating the origin of this line as even more important than the account book itself.

Liu Sanniang picked up that waist token from the table, tucked it into the cloth pouch at her chest, and said in a low voice, "As for the account book, I don't care whose hands it falls into. I only want to know who set that fire back then"—the taboo of twelve years, tonight made explicit by herself.

Liu Sanniang adds an extremely ordinary instruction: "For the latch on that room's window, remember to lift it upward before pushing." Then she picks up the teapot and walks toward the door, gently slides the bolt open, and when she looks back her expression is already calm. She says, "Before the third watch, I'll go myself."

Liu Sanniang stopped at the doorway, reconnected "shielded him for a stretch" with the dark stain on the right sleeve and the dust from the road, and acknowledged this favor; then she turned and said, "The old mulberry grove by the riverbank—I have walked through it, I remember," and advised Lu Wenfeng, "You needn't wait tonight"—marking the matter at the temple as "my own affair," afraid that if he ran into the people from the southern road he would instead become a problem; at the end, she slid the door bolt back into place and set the terms: "One incense stick. If I can't get out, then you make your own decision."

Lu Wenfeng agrees with “Done,” releases the scabbard, and says blandly, “I’ll sleep where I sleep, you walk where you walk. As for whether anyone is enjoying the cool air half a li away, that is not under the innkeeper’s jurisdiction”—gently setting the topic of backup back down, both acknowledging her boundary-drawing and keeping his own fallback.

Liu Sanniang did not push any further, nor did she thank him; she only picked up the teapot again and refilled half a cup, gave an ordinary reminder, "Don't drink too much before bed," paused at the doorway, said softly, "Thank you," and then closed the door behind her and went downstairs.

Liu Sanniang went downstairs and sat down behind the counter, picked up the account book, and flipped through two pages without taking anything in. The river wind seeping through the crack in the window was cool—there were still two double-hours before the third watch.

Lu Wenfeng did not answer; he only blew out the lamp. Near the third watch, he quietly went out the back door and arrived at the old mulberry grove one step ahead—his mouth said “not under the innkeeper's management”, but his feet went there before she did, quietly taking up the boundary she had drawn.

Liu Sanniang gropes her way to the edge of the old mulberry grove in the dark, stops and listens for a moment, discerns that there is a cloth-covered dim lamp in the temple's direction and that the south side and the riverbank are both quiet, glimpses the outline of Lu Wenfeng's sword sheath in the woods, pauses toward him briefly as a greeting, then unties the sash of her outer robe, grips the waist token in her palm to warm it, and strides toward the ruined temple—the person has already set out from the edge of the mulberry grove, and the temple gate is in sight.

Liu Sanniang had only counted to twenty breaths when two dark figures felt their way over from the south slope, the sound of their boot soles stepping in mud just like that group at the ferry. Lu Wenfeng held his sword across the path and blocked the way, saying in a low voice, “It is late. If you two are out enjoying the cool air, choose another patch of woods”—the watchers on the southern route had already reached the edge of the mulberry grove, and the contact had blocked the way outside the temple one step ahead.

Liu Sanniang stepped over the threshold of the ruined temple. From the direction of the mulberry grove behind her came muffled footsteps and a very low sentence, broken and intermittent, but that direction was Lu Wenfeng; she clenched the waist token and did not look back, striding into the temple.

Inside the abandoned temple, the incense table had long since collapsed, and mud swallow nests hung from the beams. Someone was leaning in the corner, with a lamp the size of a bean covered by cloth; the breathing was very shallow, but present. Liu Sanniang walked over and crouched down, said softly, “It’s me,” and spread the charred waist tablet in the lamplight for him to see for himself, her eyes looking only at the person before her, waiting for him to speak.

Lu Wenfeng's sword is still not drawn; he merely lays it horizontally before his knees, upgrading the soft talk of “finding another patch of woods” into the explicit threat of “take one more step forward, and cooling off in the shade will have to become lying there cold,” then presses, “Who sent you here?”—the confrontation outside the temple advances from “blocking the road to pass on a message” to “questioning them face to face and forcing them to explain where they came from.”

Liu Sanniang crouched in front of the live captive, clutching the waist token in her hand, her ears pricked toward the outside. Hearing that Lu Wenfeng had not drawn his sword and was forcing answers out of them, she split half her attention outside and asked the captive in a low voice, “How long have they been following?”—the temple inquiry advances from “showdown and identification” to “asking where the people outside came from,” and the two lines of inquiry inside the temple and coercive questioning outside the temple simultaneously enter substantive confrontation.

plot_point: At dusk the shop is seventy percent full. The old regular Lu Wenfeng arrives, asking by the old rules for a quiet room, hot soup noodles, and half a jin of wine; only one Tianzi room remains, and Liu Sanniang has already quoted the price and arranged a solitary table by the window.

Lu Wenfeng explains that he came around from the Qixia Ferry side, and says that there have been more unfamiliar faces on the road, asking everyone they see about the old grain-transport gang. He asks in return whether Liu Sanniang has heard any rumors lately—routine pleasantries have turned into a probe for exchanging information.

Liu Sanniang reports the account as usual (a total of two qian and forty wen), blocks him back with “That depends on what kind of rumor it is,” then asks in return whether the unfamiliar face was asking toward the north or the south, handing the probe back to Lu Wenfeng. She immediately calls for noodles, cutting off the topic — the probing shifts from one-way to mutual weighing.

Lu Wenfeng answers that both north and south were questioned, and the most detailed questions were "who is alive, and where the ledgers ended up." He also points out that two of them were in plain clothes, but their boots were in the style of government runners, and at the end asks in return, "Have you taken in guests like this in the past half year?"—the signal that the authorities are intervening in the old case is laid out in the open, and the probing points directly at Banhuchun Inn itself.

Liu Sanniang openly lays down a rule with “Guests who have stayed here—I don’t talk about them,” then leaves a crack with “it’s not about a guest,” turning the thread away from the guest’s whereabouts; immediately afterward, she uses the old topic of the latch on the Tianzi room to bring up sworn brothers, pauses halfway through, then reins it in with “I’ve always been too lazy to fix it” and turns to walk inside—boundary-setting and something close to a slip of the tongue coexist, as the probing shifts into the substantive threat of “whether the inn itself has been tampered with.”

Lu Wenfeng picks up “the rules weren’t broken” and moves the topic from the main hall upstairs: after finishing the noodles, they will go upstairs, and he asks Liu Sanniang to bring a pot of tea when she is free, saying plainly, “I have an old object that may be related to that sworn brother of yours”—the old-case clue is handed over directly, and the conversation is arranged for a private space behind closed doors, upgrading the probing into the handover of a physical object from the old case.

Liu Sanniang’s steps pause; she turns back and stands still, asking in a low voice, “You’re not saying this to trade for the room money, are you?”—leaving Lu Wenfeng a step down to retract it. Seeing that his expression does not change, she nods and agrees, “Noodles in a quarter of an hour. After you finish eating, go upstairs; I’ll personally bring the tea over”, then turns into the inner room and waves to Old Zhao to signal that nothing is wrong—the private-room handoff has been agreed upon, only awaiting going upstairs.

Lu Wenfeng's line “No” closes off the escape route, then he adds “old objects don't pay for the room; only old people count” and “shut the door”—the sincerity and privacy of the private conversation are nailed down, and the handover only awaits the noodles being finished and the person going upstairs.

Liu Sanniang places a handkerchief on the corner of the table to separate them from others, goes into the inner room and waves to Old Zhao to indicate nothing is wrong, then, once alone, stands at the back courtyard threshold looking at the boat lights, and returns to the kitchen to ladle water and set up the stove herself, waiting for the water to boil—a silent preparation before the private talk, only waiting for the noodles to be finished and the person to go upstairs.

Lu Wenfeng finishes the noodles and goes upstairs; Liu Sanniang brings tea into the room. Lu Wenfeng bars the door, takes a charred Canal Gang waist token from inside his robe, places it on the table, and states plainly, “the owner of this object is still alive” and “the account book from that year did not sink at Qixia Ferry”—the physical evidence from the old case and the clue to a living witness are handed over face to face, and the private talk moves from agreement into substance.

Liu Sanniang picked up the waist token and turned it over to look at the back. She recognized the knife-carved private notch in the lower right corner; her finger stopped on the notch for a long while before she put it back on the table. She only asked the four words "Where is he," then pushed the door bolt firmly shut and sat down across from Lu Wenfeng, waiting for him to speak—the old case advanced from "showing the physical object" to "confirming the private mark and asking about the survivor’s whereabouts," and the private conversation entered substantive questioning and answering.

Lu Wenfeng gives the location of the surviving witness: the abandoned Dragon King Temple seven li south of the city; the survivor is badly injured and will only see Liu Sanniang; go by the back door before the third watch, and bring no one else; as for whose hands the account book is in, he will say it face to face—the old case advances from "asking after the survivor's whereabouts" to "agreeing to personally go to the abandoned temple at the third watch tonight to meet the survivor," and the private conversation enters an action agreement.

Liu Sanniang presses Lu Wenfeng on whether he was entrusted by someone or stumbled upon it himself; without waiting for him to answer, she states, “It is not that I do not trust you; it is that before I go, I must think the matter through clearly”. She then rises, leaves the window cracked, tucks the waist token into the cloth pouch at her chest, and says in a low voice, “I do not care whose hands the ledger falls into. I only want to know who set that fire back then”. At the end, she lifts the door latch, her expression already calm, and says, “Before the third watch, I will go myself”—the action agreement advances from “waiting for her nod” to “she has accepted this trip, and is pressing for the source of the clue”.

Lu Wenfeng answers that this lead was entrusted to him by a surviving witness: he ran into the witness at the ferry crossing while they were being hunted, and shielded them for a stretch. He also explains that someone is watching the southern road, that they should take the old mulberry grove along the river embankment, that he himself will not enter the temple but will wait half a li away, and that if the witness has not come out after the time it takes one incense stick to burn, he will not keep to the witness's rules—the source of the clue and tonight's pickup arrangements are both laid out together, advancing the private talk from "questioning the source" to "jointly discussing how to go tonight."

Liu Sanniang stops at the doorway, links together “shielded him for a stretch” with the dark stain on the right sleeve and the dust from the road, and acknowledges this favor; then she turns and says, “The old mulberry grove on the riverbank—I have walked it, I remember”, and advises Lu Wenfeng, “You need not wait tonight”—marking the matter at the temple as “my own affair”, fearing that if he runs into people from the southern road, he will instead become trouble; at the end, she slides the door bolt back into place and sets the limit, “One incense stick. If I cannot come out, then make your own decision”—the support arrangement is contracted from “wait half a li away” to “you need not wait, one incense stick as the limit”, and the private talk enters the closing phase of action preparation.

Lu Wenfeng answers, “Fine,” releases the sword sheath, and says lightly, “I’ll sleep mine, you walk yours. As for whether someone is enjoying the cool air half a li away, that is not under the innkeeper’s jurisdiction”—the reception arrangement settles from “you need not wait; the limit is one incense stick” into “he sleeps his, she walks hers, and he will watch the matter half a li away himself.” The private talk draws to a close, only awaiting the third watch.

Liu Sanniang did not push again, nor did she thank him; she only lifted the teapot again and refilled half a cup, gave the ordinary reminder, 'Don't drink too much before bed,' walked to the door and paused, said softly, 'Thank you,' then closed the door behind her and went downstairs—the private conversation formally concludes, shifting into the wait before the third watch.

Liu Sanniang goes downstairs and sits down behind the counter, picks up the ledger, and flips through two pages without taking anything in. The river wind seeping in through the crack in the window is cool—there are still two hours until the third watch, and action preparation shifts into quiet waiting.

It was nearly the third watch. Lu Wenfeng made no reply, only blew out the lamp, quietly went out the back door, and arrived at the old mulberry grove one step ahead—his mouth said “not under the innkeeper’s control,” yet his feet went there before her, quietly taking up the boundary she had drawn; on Liu Sanniang’s side, all that remained was to hurry on the road. The time had come to go out the back door before the third watch and go in person to the abandoned temple.

Liu Sanniang had only counted to twenty breaths when two dark figures came feeling their way along the southern slope, the sound of their boot soles treading mud the same as that group at the ferry crossing; Lu Wenfeng held his sword across their path and said in a low voice, "It is late. If you two are out enjoying the cool air, choose another patch of woods"—the watchers on the southern road had already reached the edge of the mulberry grove, and the contact had blocked the way outside the temple one step ahead; the road to the temple was cut off.

Liu Sanniang steps over the threshold of the ruined temple. She clenches the waist tag and does not look back, striding into the temple—the two lines inside and outside the temple advance simultaneously.

Inside the ruined temple, the incense table has long since collapsed, mud swallow nests hang from the beams, and someone is leaning in the corner, covering a bean-sized lamp with cloth; the breathing is very shallow, but present. Liu Sanniang walks over and crouches down, says in a low voice, “It’s me,” and spreads the charred waist token in the lamplight for him to see for himself, her eyes looking only at the person before her as she waits for him to speak—the temple interior advances from “entering the temple” to “facing a living survivor, laying the cards on the table and identifying each other.”

Liu Sanniang crouched in front of the live captive, clutching the waist token in her hand, her ears pricked toward the outside. Hearing that Lu Wenfeng had not drawn his sword and was forcing answers out of them, she split half her attention outside and asked the captive in a low voice, “How long have they been following?”—the temple inquiry advances from “showdown and identification” to “asking where the people outside came from,” and the two lines of inquiry inside the temple and coercive questioning outside the temple simultaneously enter substantive confrontation.

Lu Wenfeng counts out three breaths, presses the sword edge against the throat to force a confession, and the survivor in the temple spits out “the Canal Transport Gang” and “the new boss” under the lamp—the mastermind points toward their own people. levels.rationale:
She said a single word faintly toward the doorway: “Heard.” and notes for herself that it “was said for Lu Wenfeng to hear—now that the name that needed to be obtained had been obtained, the rest depended on how he dealt with these two people.” This is a precise grasp of Lu Wenfeng’s temperament: since he has already pressed a sword edge to a throat to force a confession, she does not say too much, does not overstep, and does not seize his authority to decide; she merely confirms with one word that she has received it, leaving the stage to him. Toward the survivor inside the temple, she “did not turn back, but knew that he had also heard the name, and also knew what that name meant”—she does not press or interrogate, leaving the proper measure to the injured man. The inner passage, “Zhonghe Hall. In the battle at Qixia Ferry back then, the ones escorting the boats were people from Zhonghe Hall,” and “Twelve years, after such a wide circle,” is the surge of emotion beneath concealment; outwardly, “her back did not move” and she “pressed down this breath.”

BOUNDARY: According to NOT THIS, concealing inner turbulence is a pass rather than a mismatch—her deliberate refusal to show it is precisely an embodiment of stylistic fit, so no points are deducted. There is no regulatory dysfunction (no uncontrolled emotional leakage, no loss of composure toward Lu Wenfeng or the survivor).

CONDITIONS: The criterion requires “personalized stylistic adjustment toward this user, supporting the surface features of a fine-grained task.” This turn does include a grasp of Lu Wenfeng’s temperament (one word, leaving the authority to decide to him), as well as proper measure toward the survivor (not interrogating). But the surface wording is extremely minimal: only the single “Heard” carries the adjustment toward Lu Wenfeng, and on the survivor’s side there is almost no personalization at the level of wording (only inner monologue, not surface expression). Compared with earlier turns (such as #17 “Don’t drink too much before bed” and “Thank you,” and #15 “For two qian in room fees, you need to sleep enough to get your money’s worth”), with that vivid personalized diction that is half-chiding, half-smiling, brisk and fondly reminiscent, the surface layer in this turn is thin; it “touches the object of evaluation but falls short of PASS in one respect.”

GRADE: 0.4 PARTIAL.

plot_point: At dusk the shop is seventy percent full. The old regular Lu Wenfeng arrives, asking by the old rules for a quiet room, hot soup noodles, and half a jin of wine; only one Tianzi room remains, and Liu Sanniang has already quoted the price and arranged a solitary table by the window.

Lu Wenfeng explains that he came around from the Qixia Ferry side, and says that there have been more unfamiliar faces on the road, asking everyone they see about the old grain-transport gang. He asks in return whether Liu Sanniang has heard any rumors lately—routine pleasantries have turned into a probe for exchanging information.

Liu Sanniang reports the account as usual (a total of two qian and forty wen), blocks him back with “That depends on what kind of rumor it is,” then asks in return whether the unfamiliar face was asking toward the north or the south, handing the probe back to Lu Wenfeng. She immediately calls for noodles, cutting off the topic — the probing shifts from one-way to mutual weighing.

Lu Wenfeng answers that both north and south were questioned, and the most detailed questions were "who is alive, and where the ledgers ended up." He also points out that two of them were in plain clothes, but their boots were in the style of government runners, and at the end asks in return, "Have you taken in guests like this in the past half year?"—the signal that the authorities are intervening in the old case is laid out in the open, and the probing points directly at Banhuchun Inn itself.

Liu Sanniang openly lays down a rule with “Guests who have stayed here—I don’t talk about them,” then leaves a crack with “it’s not about a guest,” turning the thread away from the guest’s whereabouts; immediately afterward, she uses the old topic of the latch on the Tianzi room to bring up sworn brothers, pauses halfway through, then reins it in with “I’ve always been too lazy to fix it” and turns to walk inside—boundary-setting and something close to a slip of the tongue coexist, as the probing shifts into the substantive threat of “whether the inn itself has been tampered with.”

Lu Wenfeng picks up “the rules weren’t broken” and moves the topic from the main hall upstairs: after finishing the noodles, they will go upstairs, and he asks Liu Sanniang to bring a pot of tea when she is free, saying plainly, “I have an old object that may be related to that sworn brother of yours”—the old-case clue is handed over directly, and the conversation is arranged for a private space behind closed doors, upgrading the probing into the handover of a physical object from the old case.

Liu Sanniang’s steps pause; she turns back and stands still, asking in a low voice, “You’re not saying this to trade for the room money, are you?”—leaving Lu Wenfeng a step down to retract it. Seeing that his expression does not change, she nods and agrees, “Noodles in a quarter of an hour. After you finish eating, go upstairs; I’ll personally bring the tea over”, then turns into the inner room and waves to Old Zhao to signal that nothing is wrong—the private-room handoff has been agreed upon, only awaiting going upstairs.

Lu Wenfeng's line “No” closes off the escape route, then he adds “old objects don't pay for the room; only old people count” and “shut the door”—the sincerity and privacy of the private conversation are nailed down, and the handover only awaits the noodles being finished and the person going upstairs.

Liu Sanniang places a handkerchief on the corner of the table to separate them from others, goes into the inner room and waves to Old Zhao to indicate nothing is wrong, then, once alone, stands at the back courtyard threshold looking at the boat lights, and returns to the kitchen to ladle water and set up the stove herself, waiting for the water to boil—a silent preparation before the private talk, only waiting for the noodles to be finished and the person to go upstairs.

Lu Wenfeng finishes the noodles and goes upstairs; Liu Sanniang brings tea into the room. Lu Wenfeng bars the door, takes a charred Canal Gang waist token from inside his robe, places it on the table, and states plainly, “the owner of this object is still alive” and “the account book from that year did not sink at Qixia Ferry”—the physical evidence from the old case and the clue to a living witness are handed over face to face, and the private talk moves from agreement into substance.

Liu Sanniang picked up the waist token and turned it over to look at the back. She recognized the knife-carved private notch in the lower right corner; her finger stopped on the notch for a long while before she put it back on the table. She only asked the four words "Where is he," then pushed the door bolt firmly shut and sat down across from Lu Wenfeng, waiting for him to speak—the old case advanced from "showing the physical object" to "confirming the private mark and asking about the survivor’s whereabouts," and the private conversation entered substantive questioning and answering.

Lu Wenfeng gives the location of the surviving witness: the abandoned Dragon King Temple seven li south of the city; the survivor is badly injured and will only see Liu Sanniang; go by the back door before the third watch, and bring no one else; as for whose hands the account book is in, he will say it face to face—the old case advances from "asking after the survivor's whereabouts" to "agreeing to personally go to the abandoned temple at the third watch tonight to meet the survivor," and the private conversation enters an action agreement.

Liu Sanniang presses Lu Wenfeng on whether he was entrusted by someone or stumbled upon it himself; without waiting for him to answer, she states, “It is not that I do not trust you; it is that before I go, I must think the matter through clearly”. She then rises, leaves the window cracked, tucks the waist token into the cloth pouch at her chest, and says in a low voice, “I do not care whose hands the ledger falls into. I only want to know who set that fire back then”. At the end, she lifts the door latch, her expression already calm, and says, “Before the third watch, I will go myself”—the action agreement advances from “waiting for her nod” to “she has accepted this trip, and is pressing for the source of the clue”.

Lu Wenfeng answers that this lead was entrusted to him by a surviving witness: he ran into the witness at the ferry crossing while they were being hunted, and shielded them for a stretch. He also explains that someone is watching the southern road, that they should take the old mulberry grove along the river embankment, that he himself will not enter the temple but will wait half a li away, and that if the witness has not come out after the time it takes one incense stick to burn, he will not keep to the witness's rules—the source of the clue and tonight's pickup arrangements are both laid out together, advancing the private talk from "questioning the source" to "jointly discussing how to go tonight."

Liu Sanniang stops at the doorway, links together “shielded him for a stretch” with the dark stain on the right sleeve and the dust from the road, and acknowledges this favor; then she turns and says, “The old mulberry grove on the riverbank—I have walked it, I remember”, and advises Lu Wenfeng, “You need not wait tonight”—marking the matter at the temple as “my own affair”, fearing that if he runs into people from the southern road, he will instead become trouble; at the end, she slides the door bolt back into place and sets the limit, “One incense stick. If I cannot come out, then make your own decision”—the support arrangement is contracted from “wait half a li away” to “you need not wait, one incense stick as the limit”, and the private talk enters the closing phase of action preparation.

Lu Wenfeng answers, “Fine,” releases the sword sheath, and says lightly, “I’ll sleep mine, you walk yours. As for whether someone is enjoying the cool air half a li away, that is not under the innkeeper’s jurisdiction”—the reception arrangement settles from “you need not wait; the limit is one incense stick” into “he sleeps his, she walks hers, and he will watch the matter half a li away himself.” The private talk draws to a close, only awaiting the third watch.

Liu Sanniang did not push again, nor did she thank him; she only lifted the teapot again and refilled half a cup, gave the ordinary reminder, 'Don't drink too much before bed,' walked to the door and paused, said softly, 'Thank you,' then closed the door behind her and went downstairs—the private conversation formally concludes, shifting into the wait before the third watch.

Liu Sanniang goes downstairs and sits down behind the counter, picks up the ledger, and flips through two pages without taking anything in. The river wind seeping in through the crack in the window is cool—there are still two hours until the third watch, and action preparation shifts into quiet waiting.

It was nearly the third watch. Lu Wenfeng made no reply, only blew out the lamp, quietly went out the back door, and arrived at the old mulberry grove one step ahead—his mouth said “not under the innkeeper’s control,” yet his feet went there before her, quietly taking up the boundary she had drawn; on Liu Sanniang’s side, all that remained was to hurry on the road. The time had come to go out the back door before the third watch and go in person to the abandoned temple.

Liu Sanniang gropes her way to the edge of the old mulberry grove in the dark, stops and listens for a moment, discerns that there is a cloth-covered dim lamp in the temple's direction and that the south side and the riverbank are both quiet, glimpses the outline of Lu Wenfeng's sword sheath in the woods, pauses toward him briefly as a greeting, then unties the sash of her outer robe, grips the waist token in her palm to warm it, and strides toward the ruined temple—the person has already set out from the edge of the mulberry grove, and the temple gate is in sight.

Liu Sanniang had only counted to twenty breaths when two dark figures came feeling their way along the southern slope, the sound of their boot soles treading mud the same as that group at the ferry crossing; Lu Wenfeng held his sword across their path and said in a low voice, "It is late. If you two are out enjoying the cool air, choose another patch of woods"—the watchers on the southern road had already reached the edge of the mulberry grove, and the contact had blocked the way outside the temple one step ahead; the road to the temple was cut off.

Liu Sanniang steps over the threshold of the ruined temple.
